record.paper_title: Models, feedback control, and open problems of 3D bipedal robotic walking
record.original_question: Find impact models, even approximate ones, for the inelastic collision of the swing leg with the ground that allow a nontrivial double-support phase in robots with stiff feet and limbs. The intended outcome is a hybrid impact model that can represent walking gaits closer to human walking, where double support occupies a significant portion of the gait cycle.

evidence.quote: Work in Miossec and Aoustin [2002] indicates that the approach currently used to represent an inelastic impact of the swing leg with the ground essentially rules out a nontrivial double support phase.
It would be very useful to find impact models, even very approximate ones, that will allow such gaits in robots with “stiff” feet and limbs.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a planar or three-dimensional bipedal robot modeled as a rigid open kinematic chain with stiff (non-compliant) feet and limbs. Walking is described as a hybrid dynamical system that alternates between continuous-time phases (single support, double support) and discrete impact events corresponding to the swing leg striking the ground.

The standard rigid-body impact model treats the foot-ground collision as an instantaneous, perfectly inelastic impulsive event: the impact map is derived from conservation of generalized momentum subject to the algebraic constraint that the impacting foot has zero velocity immediately after impact (and, in many formulations, that the previous stance foot lifts off). Under this standard model, it can be shown that any nontrivial double-support phase, in which both feet remain in stationary ground contact for a positive time interval while the configuration evolves, is essentially precluded for a robot with stiff feet and limbs.

Problem: Construct an impact model — exact or approximate — for the inelastic collision of the swing leg with the ground in a rigid bipedal robot with stiff feet and limbs, such that the resulting hybrid model admits periodic walking gaits with a nontrivial (positive-duration) double-support phase occupying a substantial fraction of the gait cycle, in qualitative agreement with human walking. Specify the post-impact velocity reset map, the contact constraints active during double support, the conditions for transition into and out of double support, and verify that the resulting hybrid model is physically consistent (energy-non-increasing, satisfies unilateral contact constraints with non-negative normal forces and friction-cone conditions) and admits at least one stable periodic gait with a nontrivial double-support sub-phase.
artifact.category_tag: hybrid impact models for bipedal walking
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent work has proposed impact models and control frameworks (e.g., extensions of hybrid zero dynamics with non-instantaneous double support, compliant/spring-mass approximations, and underactuated walkers generating non-instantaneous double-limb support motion) that produce gaits with a nontrivial double-support phase. However, a fully satisfactory rigid-body impact model for stiff-footed/stiff-limbed robots that yields human-like, substantial double-support durations remains an active research topic rather than a settled matter.

status_evidence.title: Hybrid Zero Dynamics Control for Bipedal Walking with a Non-Instantaneous Double Support Phase
status_evidence.snippet: Extends hybrid zero dynamics to include a non-instantaneous double support phase, addressing the standard assumption of instantaneous double support.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work develops hybrid models with nontrivial double-support phases, indicating partial progress on the problem.

status_evidence.title: Stability and efficiency of underactuated bipedal walker that generates non-instantaneous double-limb support motion
status_evidence.snippet: Underactuated bipedal walker generates non-instantaneous double-limb support motion.
status_evidence.claim: Models producing nontrivial double-support phases have been constructed, supporting partial-solved status.

status_evidence.title: Compliant leg behaviour explains basic dynamics of walking and running
status_evidence.snippet: Compliant legs are essential to obtain the basic walking mechanics including double support; stiff legs do not reproduce walking dynamics.
status_evidence.claim: Stiff-legged rigid impact models inherently struggle to produce nontrivial double support, confirming the difficulty noted in the original problem.
